extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and advanced students interested in algebraic and projective geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Derivations and theorems about how a straight line (transversal) is cut by algebraic surfaces (of given degree), giving algebraic relations between the segments, involution/anharmonic relations, loci of centres of involution, and related projective properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between product of principal semi-axes and coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute term of the characteristic equation equals the product of the squares of the principal semi-axes of the ellipsoid. Hence if A, B, C be the principal semi-axes of (1), one of the relations in question is ABC = abc^(1 - /»--A*-./+2/^^)*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from eliminating variables after substituting the eigenvalue \=5^ into the system (5),(6),(7) and observing that the absolute term equals the product of squares of the principal semi-axes. A reference to Gregory's Solid Geometry (page 88) is given for another investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse properties via conjugate diameters (equations (4) and (5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Referring an ellipse to two conjugate diameters as oblique axes leads to equations (1) and (2); differentiating and eliminating gives r_i r_j = aJ sin ^ (equation (4)), and relation (5) — r^J^r^-a^^h^ — expressing another property of conjugate/ principal semi-axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The properties alluded to are contained in (4) and (5). The derivation uses expressing radius r in coordinates relative to oblique axes, differentiating, and applying the theory of equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXVIII: Ratio of continued products of segments by a surface of degree n
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line AP be cut by a given surface of the n^ degree in the points Q1, Q2, ... Qn, then the compounded ratio P Q1 . P Q2 . ... P Qn : A Q1 . A Q2 . ... A Qn (denoted (PQn):(AQn)) can be expressed in terms of the coordinates of P by writing the polar equation of the surface and substituting roots p1,...,pn, yielding (PQn):(AQn) = 1 + r f1(λ,μ,ν) + r^2 f2(λ,μ,ν) + ... + r^n fn(λ,μ,ν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here λ, μ, ν are the direction cosines of the radius vector; when n is even the sign is positive, when n is odd the sign is negative (upper or lower sign according as n is even or odd). The notation (PQn) denotes continued product PQ1·PQ2·...·PQn.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXIX: Surfaces through intersection of two surfaces and involution relation (equation (3))
rubrics_metrics.description: If u=0 and v=0 are two surfaces and p a constant, surfaces of the form u = p v represent surfaces of degree n passing through their intersection. For a transversal meeting u=0 in Qi, v=0 in Ri, and u=pv in Pi, substituting into u=pv gives (PiQn)(ARn) = ± p (PiRn)(AQn), and eliminating leads to (PiQn)(PiRn) = (PiQn)(PiRn) (equation (3)), showing the points Q and R together with Pi and Pj form a system of m+n+2 points in involution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, if a surface of degree n passes through the intersection of two surfaces not exceeding degree n, then for any transversal the points at which it cuts any two of the surfaces and any two of the points at which it cuts the third are in involution. Counts of combinations of such involutions are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXX: Anharmonic and harmonic functions of collections of points (equation (4) and (5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two surfaces u=0, v=0 and constructed surfaces u = i p v and u = p' v, for a transversal meeting them in Pi,... and Ri,... and Si,... one obtains (RlPn)(SiPn)/(RiQn)(SiQn) = p/p' (equation (4)). When specialized to planes this reduces to the anharmonic relation of four points; for p' = -p this yields harmonic relations (equation (5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first member of (4) is called the anharmonic function of n+2 points and the expression generalizes Chasles' anharmonic ratio; symmetry/counting remarks: the anharmonic function of 2n+2 points may be expressed in 3n different ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXI: Enveloping surfaces and system of four harmonic radial surfaces (theorem xxx)
rubrics_metrics.description: If three surfaces of degree n touch a given surface of degree m along curves of intersection with two other surfaces (of degree m and r respectively, with 2m ≤ n and r ≤ m), then their enveloping surfaces intersect in two surfaces of degree m which pass through the curves of contact and together with them form a system of four harmonic radial surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is analogous to Monge's system. When the two contact-surfaces coincide a 'curve of contact' and first-order contact descriptions appear; explicit algebraic forms (7),(7') and resolution into two surfaces (8) are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXII: Equation of surface of degree n through m given plane sections (equation (9))
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f=0 be a surface of degree n and v1=0,...,vm=0 given planes (m ≤ n). Then the equation of a surface of degree n passing through the m plane sections of f is U = z = p v1 v2 ... vm (equation (9)), where p is constant and z a function of x,y,z of degree ≤ n - m. This surface passes through the m plane curves and through the intersection of f with z=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special cases: when m = n - 1 the function is linear and the surface is a plane; counting and involution relations for the points where a transversal meets these surfaces are given (equation (10)).

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXIII: Plane contact and contact order consequences (equations (11)–(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the planes v1,...,vm coincide with a single plane v and is constant, equation (9) reduces to u = p v^i and the curves of intersection unite in a curve of contact of order (m−1). Equations (11),(11') describe surfaces having a contact of order (m−1) with t=0; resolving differences gives decomposition into surfaces or planes depending on parity of m and contact order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: if two surfaces of degree n have a plane contact with a given surface of degree n, their intersections lie upon two planes, or one plane passing through the intersection of the planes of contact, according as the contact order is odd or even. Fixed-point consequences when surface passes through two points are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXIV: Centre of involution locus when intersection lies on surface of degree n−1 (equation (12) and (13))
rubrics_metrics.description: For equations f=0 (degree n), t=0 (degree n−1) the family w = p r (equation (12)) denotes surfaces of degree n passing through the intersection and cutting f in a plane curve of degree n at infinity. For a transversal meeting these, one finds that points Ri at infinity are centres of involution of the 2n points P and Q (equation (13)). Thus the surface of degree n−1 may be the locus of centres of involution for two degree-n surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This holds also when the surface at infinity is complex (e.g. composed of n−1 planes).

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXV: Surface of degree n through m·n intersections of m+n planes (equation (14) and counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given m+n planes, a surface of degree n passing through m·n of their intersections has equation (14) = U = z = p v1 v2 ... v_{m+n}? (text gives general form), with p constant and z function of degree ≤ n−m. The surface passes through m·n straight lines; counts and combinatorial numbers of such systems are given; special cases m=n and m=n−1 discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When some planes coincide the mn lines unite in n lines of contact and equation becomes (16) representing a surface touching given planes along those lines. Involution relations for segments when a transversal meets these surfaces are given (equation (15)).

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXVI: Locus of a point Pi given product relation of directed segments (equation (18))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given several surfaces of various degrees and a straight line APi meeting each in sequences of points, choosing Pi such that PiQi·PiRi·PiSi·... equals a similar continued product gives the locus equation (xxviii) 1 − K1 + tta − tt3 ± ... = 0 (equation (18)), showing the locus of Pi is a surface of degree w* (text notation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The section treats first the two-surface case in detail; elimination of parameters yields linear relations like (19) expressing properties of algebraic surfaces akin to involution relations. It explains how to derive multiple independent equations by taking combinations of different transversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXVII: Generalization — polar/Taylor expansion expression of (PQn):(AQn) (equation (a') )
rubrics_metrics.description: For a surface u=f(x,y,z)=0 and a transversal AP with AP=r and direction cosines λ,μ,ν, Taylor expansion (polar equation) about A shows (PQn):(AQn) = u' where u' = f(x',y',z') with x',y',z' the coordinates of P relative to A (equation (a')). When n is even sign positive, when odd sign negative; generally PQ1·...·PQn / (AQ1·...·AQn) = ± u'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general polar/Taylor approach allows deducing most general properties of transversals; examples and a demonstration that these results hold for transcendental curves/surfaces as well are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXXVIII–XL: Consequences and applications (polygon segment-product invariance, transcendental example, multi-point loci)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications include: (20)-(23) — for polygon sides cut by a transversal surface of degree v, the continued product of the conterminous segments measured from polygon vertices remains invariant when order reversed; specialization to planes yields Carnot's results. XXXIX demonstrates applicability to transcendental curves (quadratrix), deriving infinite product formulas. XL gives a multi-point locus problem leading to equation (26) u' v' = p w' describing loci touching given surfaces along intersection curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate how general equation (I)/(20) can yield classical theorems (Carnot), handle transcendental cases, and produce loci equations for points M whose secants have prescribed continued product relations. The text indicates further generalizations and that these methods extend to projective properties and more general central projection theories (Poncelet homologiques etc.).
